title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition leads with SpaceX catching the upper stage of its Starship rocket for the first time, and with the fallout from Friday's nationwide US flight ground stop, which officials linked to a contractor's equipment upgrade. It also covers investor pressure at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's resignation, a tanker crash on the Mississippi in New Orleans, a bomb found at an Illinois ethanol plant, and the first Eurovision Asia. Shorter items cover a Concord house fire, North Korea-linked hacking targets and an AI exam-cheating confession in South Korea.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage with launch tower for first time; booster lost
stories.summary: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with the mechanical arms of its Texas launch tower after a flight of about 22 hours, the first time it has recovered that part of the vehicle this way. The 15th test flight was meant to recover both stages, but the Super Heavy booster aborted its planned catch minutes after Friday's launch, diverted over the water and exploded. In orbit, the ship deployed 26 Starlink satellites and circled Earth 14 times before returning to Starbase on Saturday. SpaceX is still investigating the booster failure. The program matters to NASA's plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028.
key_facts: 15th Starship test flight; the first attempt to catch both stages
The upper stage completed 14 orbits and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites
SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy booster on three earlier flights
The booster exploded over the Gulf after an automated abort; Musk said it was "slightly low on fuel"
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised the flight on X: "Making more believers by the day"

perspectives.framing: The Guardian called it a victory and a milestone toward human spaceflight. It quoted a SpaceX spokesperson explaining the booster abort, and it noted that Isaacman is a Musk ally whom Musk advised Trump to appoint. It also tied Starship to Musk's 'satellite internet empire.' The Verge focused on the catch itself, called it a milestone though not a complete success, and suggested the booster failure was not insurmountable.

BBC and CNBC covered the economics of reusability and the stakes for NASA's 2028 Moon timeline and for SpaceX shareholders now that the company is public. BBC quoted an aerospace expert who called the booster loss a setback but the ship recovery a substantial step. CNBC added that Hawaii briefly paused some flights over debris risk.

Fox Business framed it as SpaceX 'making history.' It highlighted praise from Musk biographer Walter Isaacson and War Secretary Pete Hegseth, who called Musk 'a great American.' The Washington Examiner ran the AP account, which called the return 'triumphant' while noting the missed double catch.

disputed: Why the booster failed: Musk said it was low on fuel, a SpaceX spokesperson said guidance systems found it out of position for a catch, and Fox Business reported its engines shut down prematurely. Engineers are still investigating.
Whether SpaceX can recover both stages reliably on the same flight has not yet been shown.
stories.why: A fully reusable Starship could sharply cut launch costs, and NASA's crewed Moon landing plans depend on it.

stories.headline: Nvidia investors urge careful CEO search, including a possible Huang return
stories.summary: Two major Nvidia shareholders, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker, asked the board to take a slow, deliberate approach to choosing a permanent leader and to consider 'the potential return of Jensen Huang.' Huang resigned Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman described as a suspected Chinese spy who worked with Megaspeed, a Singapore company under Justice Department investigation over possible diversion of restricted chips to China. Former CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. Elon Musk said he signed a petition to reinstate Huang and warned that 'critical deals will be lost' without him. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, and Huang has also been asked to testify.
key_facts: Huang resigned Thursday; Colette Kress, CFO for 13 years, is interim CEO
Altimeter held about 9.4 million Nvidia shares worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30
The investor letter did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement
Lutnick is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing

perspectives.framing: CNBC reported the investor letter, the petition and Musk's comments, along with the congressional testimony requests and Trump's upcoming China trip. TechCrunch asked what Nvidia's security team knew. It noted turnover in the chief security officer role while saying nothing publicly links that change to Megaspeed, and it quoted a former intelligence officer on how affairs can give foreign spies leverage.

A New York Post column used the episode to defend short sellers. It described the woman as someone 'the feds believe could be a Chinese spy,' argued the ouster exposed governance flaws, and quoted an anonymous short seller who said the 'AI cycle is over.' The Washington Examiner headlined investors pushing for Huang's reinstatement and framed the departure as sparking a political battle inside the Trump administration.

disputed: The espionage suspicion about Alice Huang is reported but unproven, and Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.
The 'Stand with Jensen' petition's claim of more than 100,000 signatures, including over 5,000 Nvidia employees, is unverified.
Musk's claim that many supply deals were handshake agreements with Huang has not been confirmed.
Outlets differ on emphasis: the Examiner says investors 'push for' reinstatement, while CNBC notes the letter did not call for it immediately.
It is unclear what Nvidia's security team or board knew about the Megaspeed inquiry and Huang's relationships.
stories.why: Leadership at one of the world's most valuable chip companies is tied up with US-China tech export controls and wider AI market confidence.

stories.headline: Philippines' Carmelle wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok
stories.summary: Nineteen-year-old Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok with 'Sobra-Sobra,' a song about female empowerment sung in Tagalog and English. Eleven countries competed, with hosts Thailand second and Vietnam third. China, Japan and India did not take part, tickets were still available hours before the show, and the arena was not full. Organisers say it may take years for the contest to establish itself.
key_facts: Philippines won with 211 points: 93 from juries and 118 from the public
Thailand finished second with 170 points and Vietnam third with 164
11 countries took part; voting was split 50/50 between juries and the public
Eurovision drew 131 million viewers in 2026, down 35 million after a boycott by five countries over Israel's participation
The winner receives a trophy but no prize money

perspectives.framing: The Guardian focused on Carmelle's personal story and the staging of each act, including Nepal's singer appealing for support after deadly floods. It also explained the voting details, including paid extra votes, and Laos's technical problems.

BBC, DW and CNA covered the results and festive atmosphere but questioned the contest's staying power, pointing to a thin local turnout, unsold tickets, absent major nations and the failed US spinoff. CNA noted the Israel-related boycott in Europe, which organisers say is unrelated to the expansion.

disputed: Accounts of Laos's broadcast mishap differ: BBC says a music video was replayed over an apparent technical issue, while the Guardian says her dress rehearsal was aired after the live performances.
Whether regional broadcasters will commit to future editions is unclear.
stories.why: It tests whether one of the world's biggest TV music events can grow beyond Europe.

stories.headline: New Orleans port sues tanker owners after collision capsizes docked riverboat
stories.summary: A tanker, the Atlantic Asphalt, appeared to lose steering near the Crescent City Connection bridge on Friday and struck the docked paddlewheel cruise ship American Heritage, which capsized and partly sank. Everyone aboard survived; 32 people were taken to hospitals and eight remained hospitalized Saturday. The Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit alleging negligence and at least $1 million in terminal damage, and a judge authorized seizure of the tanker. The NTSB has recovered the tanker's voyage data recorder and expects a preliminary report in about 30 days, while the Coast Guard says removing the cruise ship will take weeks.
key_facts: The lawsuit names the tanker, owner Nave Shipping SA and manager Thome Ship Management
Chief US District Judge Wendy Vitter granted the request to arrest the vessel
Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation
16,000 gallons of fuel must be removed from the American Heritage before salvage
The NTSB final report is expected in 18 to 24 months

perspectives.framing: PBS, running the AP account, led with the port suing to seize a vessel 'owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.' It featured a survivor's account of being thrown into the river and details of the NTSB investigation.
BBC and WBTV focused on the lawsuit's details and the officials' 'miracle on the Mississippi' description. BBC also noted the Chinese parent company and that it had requested comment.

Fox News emphasized the rescue: about 100 people pulled from the river, the injured captain who was last to leave, and the Coast Guard saying there was no indication of terrorism. Fox Business focused on the lawsuit and seizure, and noted it was unclear whether the warrant had been executed.

disputed: Reported numbers aboard vary: 192 passengers, 197 passengers and crew, 191 passengers and crew, or about 129 passengers plus crew.
Fox reported two people in serious condition, while other outlets said no injuries were critical.
The cause is unconfirmed; officials point to a possible steering loss.
Fox Business said it was unclear whether the warrant had been executed, while PBS reported federal officials had control of the ship.
stories.why: The crash disrupted traffic on a major US shipping artery and raises questions about vessel safety and liability.

stories.headline: Stranded travelers face weekend disruption after nationwide ground stop
stories.summary: Travelers at airports including Charlotte Douglas spent Friday night on floors and benches after the FAA halted all US flights for several hours. Passengers described missed funerals, lost bookings and little information from airlines or the FAA. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging legacy equipment. FAA officials expect schedules to return to normal by the end of Sunday.
key_facts: Only the second nationwide ground stop of its kind since 9/11, and described as the longest
FAA chief Bryan Bedford said crews and aircraft were out of position after 12,000 lost flights
American Airlines said it was prioritizing international flights and flights to non-hub airports

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera focused on the official explanation, Duffy's vow to 'hold people accountable,' L3Harris's response and the denial of a cyberattack. The Guardian's video piece noted that the homeland security and transportation secretaries suggested older technology was overwhelmed.
WBTV centered on frustrated Charlotte passengers and their complaints about poor communication from airlines and the FAA. The Hill ran live updates on the recovery.

disputed: Reported duration varies from about four hours to nearly five.
The root cause is still under investigation.
stories.why: Knock-on disruption is still affecting travelers ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period.

stories.headline: Duffy links ground stop to L3Harris upgrade, says cause is still being determined
stories.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday's ground stop followed routine work by contractor L3Harris to switch a remote FAA telecom line from copper to fiber. He said a router then flooded other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and communications. Duffy said officials are still determining whether the cause was installer error or a faulty router, and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was 'zero evidence' of anything nefarious or AI-related. L3Harris said it is supporting the investigation and has completed more than 70% of the conversion. Duffy used the moment to press Congress for more modernization money.
key_facts: Duffy said L3Harris owns the FAA's legacy telecom network and has worked for the agency for over 20 years
Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control modernization in July 2025
About 9,000 US flights were canceled Friday, according to FlightAware
Duffy said AT&T, Verizon and Lumen will work on the new architecture

perspectives.framing: NPR and The Verge reported Duffy's account and L3Harris's full statement, and noted his renewed funding request and his description of a 'partial payment' from Congress.
CNBC placed the outage within the wider struggle with aging infrastructure. It included Bedford's explanation for grounding flights and how airlines are offering crews extra pay to recover.
Fox Business profiled L3Harris and emphasized Duffy appearing to blame the company and saying he is 'stuck' with it. The Washington Examiner framed the story as Duffy criticizing the contractor.

disputed: Whether L3Harris error or faulty equipment caused the failure has not been determined.
Friday delay counts differ: CNBC reported more than 7,000 and NPR nearly 25,000.
stories.why: The outage puts a spotlight on fragile air traffic infrastructure and on the coming funding fight in Congress.

stories.headline: Two-alarm fire destroys Concord home; no injuries
stories.summary: Concord firefighters responded shortly after midnight Saturday to a two-story house fire on Millstone Circle SW and brought it under control at 1:16 a.m. No one was injured. The Red Cross is helping the displaced family, and the fire marshal is investigating the cause.
key_facts: Dispatched at 12:21 a.m.; second alarm at 12:32 a.m.
36 firefighters from Concord and Harrisburg responded

perspectives.framing: Local Charlotte stations gave straightforward incident reports.

disputed: Cause under investigation.
stories.why: It is a local safety incident for Cabarrus County residents.

stories.headline: Bomb found at Peoria ethanol plant; evacuation lifted after search
stories.summary: Authorities found a bomb at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, on Friday and rendered it safe. A one-mile evacuation zone covering parts of Peoria and East Peoria was in place overnight. After a search found no other devices, police lifted the order Saturday afternoon. The FBI and ATF are investigating, and no arrests have been announced.
key_facts: The evacuation covered a one-mile radius and was lifted around 1 p.m. Saturday
About 60 to 80 people stayed at a shelter at Manual High School
No injuries were reported
Mayor Rita Ali confirmed the device was a bomb

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and NPR stressed officials' insistence that the threat was real, not a hoax, and the FBI's vow to find whoever was responsible. They also covered local cancellations. NPR noted that most bomb threats do not prove credible.
WBTV focused on the lifted evacuation and official statements.

disputed: The type of device and any motive or suspect have not been disclosed.
Accounts differ on whether the device was found Friday afternoon or Friday night.
stories.why: A confirmed bomb at a plant holding combustible chemicals is a serious public safety threat.

stories.headline: Security firm says North Korea-linked hackers listed 30 South Korean servers as targets
stories.summary: Cybersecurity firm Cyfirma says it obtained a list of 216 servers in 10 countries, compiled in October by Korean-speaking hackers it links with 'high confidence' to North Korea's Lazarus Group. Thirty of the servers are in South Korea. The targets include government agencies, banks, telecoms and infrastructure providers. Cyfirma said being on the list does not mean a server was breached.
key_facts: The list was completed Oct. 24
148 targets were in Asia-Pacific, 49 in North America and 19 in the Middle East
The US and Japan accounted for 44.4% of the targets

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and the Korea Herald ran the same report, relaying Cyfirma's findings and its advice to patch and restart affected programs.

disputed: The attribution comes from a single private firm, and no breaches are confirmed.
stories.why: It points to continued state-linked cyber threats against critical infrastructure in several countries.

stories.headline: Top scorer on South Korean tax accountant exam confesses to AI-assisted cheating
stories.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, who placed first on South Korea's tax accountant exam, turned himself in to Seoul police. In a video, he admitted using a miniature camera to photograph questions, sending them to an AI tool and reading the answers on a smartphone. He also admitted cheating the same way on the first round of the CPA exam in March. He had earlier denied the allegations, which arose from scores far above the average.
key_facts: He scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round
The average score in introductory tax law was 30.18; he scored a perfect 100
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed zero tolerance for exam cheating

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald detailed his confession, his statistically unusual scores and his earlier denials.

disputed: Legal consequences and any changes to exam security are still pending.
stories.why: The case shows how AI tools are creating new cheating risks for high-stakes professional exams.
